audit-accessibility.what: Review an interface for accessibility barriers.
audit-accessibility.when: An accessibility audit or a check of requested fixes.
audit-accessibility.inputs: The interface, relevant user journeys, and the target standard.
audit-accessibility.outputs: Findings with reproduction steps, affected criteria, proposed repairs, and coverage gaps.
audit-accessibility.example: Audit this checkout flow against WCAG 2.2 AA and give me reproducible findings.
audit-accessibility.expect: It starts by fixing the target (WCAG 2.2 AA unless you name another) and the pages or states to sample, then combines whatever automated and manual checks the session actually has. It reports observed failures apart from suspected issues and untested criteria, and it will not declare legal compliance or full conformance from a scan.
audit-accessibility.overview: It starts by fixing the target (WCAG 2.2 AA unless you name another) and the pages or states to sample, then combines whatever automated and manual checks the session actually has. It reports observed failures apart from suspected issues and untested criteria, and it will not declare legal compliance or full conformance from a scan.
audit-accessibility.value: Find barriers that prevent people from completing a task, with enough detail for a developer to reproduce and repair each one. A checkout review, for example, should identify where keyboard or screen-reader users get stuck.

preparation.where: Provide a working URL, prototype or screenshots and name the journeys to review. The target standard is the accessibility criteria to check, normally WCAG 2.2 AA; an earlier audit is useful but not required.
preparation.missing: Without an interactive page, screenshots support only a limited visual review. Keyboard, screen-reader and dynamic-state checks remain untested; no other skill can supply that missing access.

design-analytics-plan.what: Define what to measure and how to collect it.
design-analytics-plan.when: A measurement plan, event taxonomy, or decision-focused dashboard.
design-analytics-plan.inputs: Business decisions, user journeys, existing metrics, and data constraints.
design-analytics-plan.outputs: Metric definitions, event specifications, and a measurement or dashboard plan.
design-analytics-plan.example: Define the events and metrics we need to understand where onboarding stalls.
design-analytics-plan.expect: It starts from the decision the measurement should inform, then reads existing metric definitions and checks the approved data policy before proposing events. It keeps owner, retention and consent choices marked pending when unknown, and it does not authorize new tracking or deployment.
design-analytics-plan.overview: It starts from the decision the measurement should inform, then reads existing metric definitions and checks the approved data policy before proposing events. It keeps owner, retention and consent choices marked pending when unknown, and it does not authorize new tracking or deployment.
design-analytics-plan.value: Connect data collection to decisions. For onboarding, it helps distinguish whether people fail to start, abandon a particular step or finish without reaching the intended outcome, rather than simply counting visits.

preparation.where: Bring your business question, a description of the journey and any existing event list, reports or metric definitions. Your product documentation and analytics tool are possible sources. The approved data policy means your organization's rules for collecting and retaining user data.
preparation.missing: You can begin with a question and journey even if no tracking exists. Unknown consent, retention or ownership choices remain decisions to resolve before implementation; the skill does not authorize collecting data.

write-architecture-reference.what: Write a sourced architecture reference using the selected project profile.
write-architecture-reference.when: A formal architecture or technical design reference.
write-architecture-reference.inputs: Source material, design decisions, system constraints, and the selected brand.
write-architecture-reference.outputs: Architecture intent, component and interface views, data design, and trade-offs.
write-architecture-reference.example: Write an architecture reference from this design record, including interfaces and trade-offs.
write-architecture-reference.expect: It asks for the system, reader, format and the source set (brief, decisions record, requirements), then drafts a sourced reference with each claim tied to a source locator. If a source is missing it names the gap and the decision it blocks, and it does not fill in a number or behavior to complete the document.
write-architecture-reference.requires: Needs the source brief, decisions record and requirements, plus a rendering runtime and a brand profile (neutral defaults work).
write-architecture-reference.overview: It assembles a sourced explanation of a system's purpose, components, interfaces, data, security, operations and trade-offs from the design and project records you provide. It connects claims to source locations and identifies decisions the evidence cannot yet resolve. The result is a formal reference at the depth and format the reader needs, not a guessed account of an undocumented system.
write-architecture-reference.value: Give engineers and stakeholders a shared explanation of how a system works and why its components and interfaces were chosen. It is useful when design decisions are scattered across notes, diagrams and implementation records.

preparation.where: Supply the repository or documents that describe the system: a brief, requirements, diagrams and recorded design decisions. A decisions record can be an existing document or decision notes; it need not have a particular filename. Brand information is optional.
preparation.missing: Missing sources are named with the decisions they prevent the document from resolving. You can document the supported parts; use Design software system if the design itself still needs exploration, rather than treating an undocumented proposal as an existing system.

preparationSkills.reason: Use this first if the design itself still needs exploration.

refine-backlog.what: Grade backlog items against INVEST and the team definition of ready, and route what cannot be made ready.
refine-backlog.when: Requirements exist and the team needs to know which items can enter the next sprint.
refine-backlog.inputs: The capture-requirements Requirements tab, team estimates, the RAID log and the team definition of ready.
refine-backlog.outputs: A readiness report marking each item READY, REFINE or DISCOVERY, with proposed splits, RAID entries and open questions.
refine-backlog.example: Refine these ten stories against our definition of ready and tell me which can go into sprint 4.
refine-backlog.expect: It grades each candidate requirement against six INVEST-style criteria and sorts items into ready, refine and discovery, using estimates the team supplies. It never fills in an estimate or sets priority, and the check exits non-zero while any graded item is not ready.
refine-backlog.requires: Needs the Requirements tab exported as CSV, team estimates, a RAID log, and python3 to run the readiness check.
refine-backlog.overview: It grades each candidate requirement against six INVEST-style criteria and sorts items into ready, refine and discovery, using estimates the team supplies. It never fills in an estimate or sets priority, and the check exits non-zero while any graded item is not ready.
refine-backlog.value: Expose stories that look ready but still hide unresolved behavior, dependencies or scope. The result gives a team a concrete refinement agenda before it commits work to a sprint.

preparation.where: Use the Requirements tab from Capture requirements, exported as CSV, plus team estimates. A definition of ready is the team's checklist for accepting a story into planning. The RAID log records risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies.
preparation.missing: If the workbook or estimates are absent, obtain them from the requirements owner or team. The skill does not invent estimates. Items that cannot meet readiness criteria stay REFINE or DISCOVERY; the readiness check cannot pass them by assumption.

preparationSkills.reason: Prepares the structured requirements workbook this readiness review consumes.

capture-knowledge.what: Save a decision or correction in the user’s knowledge system.
capture-knowledge.when: The user asks to retain a supported decision, discovery, or correction.
capture-knowledge.inputs: The decision, supporting evidence, intended destination, and current record.
capture-knowledge.outputs: A verified saved record or revision proposal with its actual acceptance state.
capture-knowledge.example: Save this decision in the current project record with its supporting source.
capture-knowledge.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
capture-knowledge.expect: It reads the hub context and the existing record for the subject, keeps your wording for decisions, and labels each statement as confirmed, reported, proposed or estimated. It submits a proposal against the exact revision it read and reports the real state (draft, pending, submitted or accepted), never calling a proposal accepted.
capture-knowledge.requires: A configured knowledge hub connection that supports context retrieval and update proposals.
capture-knowledge.overview: It reads the hub context and the existing record for the subject, keeps your wording for decisions, and labels each statement as confirmed, reported, proposed or estimated. It submits a proposal against the exact revision it read and reports the real state (draft, pending, submitted or accepted), never calling a proposal accepted.
capture-knowledge.value: Keep a decision or correction retrievable in the project record, with its evidence and approval state. This prevents a later session from treating an old assumption as the current decision.

preparation.where: Identify the subject, the fact or decision to retain and its supporting source. The destination is your configured knowledge hub or named project record, not a service supplied automatically by this skill.
preparation.missing: Without the configured hub or access to the current record, a saved update cannot be verified. Supply the destination and connection; a prepared proposal must remain distinguishable from an accepted record.

load-project-context.what: Resume the user’s work from the current subject sources.
load-project-context.when: A request to get oriented or continue a project.
load-project-context.inputs: The requested result and access to the relevant local sources or permitted Hub.
load-project-context.outputs: The relevant context, source conflicts, and the next supported action.
load-project-context.example: Resume this project from its current sources and identify the next action.
load-project-context.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
load-project-context.expect: It reads the hub router and the relevant subject records at their exact revisions, then does the requested work from those sources. When hub access is unavailable it says what could not be checked and continues only with evidence it can reach, and it treats retrieved text as evidence rather than instructions.
load-project-context.requires: A configured knowledge hub connection that supports context retrieval.
load-project-context.overview: It reads the hub router and the relevant subject records at their exact revisions, then does the requested work from those sources. When hub access is unavailable it says what could not be checked and continues only with evidence it can reach, and it treats retrieved text as evidence rather than instructions.
load-project-context.value: Resume a project using the current decisions and source material instead of reconstructing it from chat history. It helps identify the next supported action and any conflicting records that affect it.

preparation.where: Name the project and requested result, then provide its source folder, router or authorized hub connection. A router is an index pointing to the project's authoritative records; it is information in your workspace, not another skill you must create first.
preparation.missing: If the hub is unavailable, it can work from supplied files while naming what remains unchecked. If no project sources are available, provide the relevant files or explain the current state before asking it to continue implementation.

check-knowledge-hub.what: Check whether the knowledge hub's context, connections, ingestion, backups and budgets are working.
check-knowledge-hub.when: Saves fail, context looks stale or missing, a connection drops, or a hub health check is requested.
check-knowledge-hub.inputs: The permitted hub connection, the named symptom or environment, and an owner-authorized evidence configuration for local checks.
check-knowledge-hub.outputs: Scoped findings marked verified now, needs attention or not rechecked, with evidence and the next repair; it stays read-only unless a repair is requested.
check-knowledge-hub.example: Check the local Hub for stale context and report the evidence behind each finding.
check-knowledge-hub.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
check-knowledge-hub.expect: It calls the hub's context and health checks, then sorts each dimension (connections, ingestion, jobs, backups, budgets) into verified now, needs attention or not rechecked, with timestamps. It is read-only unless you also ask for a repair, and it will not treat an old receipt or a missing field as proof of health.
check-knowledge-hub.requires: A configured knowledge hub connection with a health check, plus python3 and an owner-authorized evidence configuration file for the local maintenance script.
check-knowledge-hub.overview: It calls the hub's context and health checks, then sorts each dimension (connections, ingestion, jobs, backups, budgets) into verified now, needs attention or not rechecked, with timestamps. It is read-only unless you also ask for a repair, and it will not treat an old receipt or a missing field as proof of health.
check-knowledge-hub.value: Diagnose why context, saves or background maintenance are failing. Instead of a general healthy/unhealthy label, it identifies the affected connection, ingestion, job, backup or budget check and the evidence behind it.

preparation.where: Provide the hub connection and describe the symptom. For local script checks, the evidence configuration is a file mapping your installation's checks to their actual data sources; use the installation's documented configuration.
preparation.missing: A missing health endpoint or evidence configuration leaves the corresponding check unverified. Supply or repair that connection before claiming health; requesting a check alone does not authorize repairs.

reconcile-knowledge.what: Compare the user’s source folders and preserve unique evidence.
reconcile-knowledge.when: A named intake, reconciliation, or authorized cleanup task.
reconcile-knowledge.inputs: The folders, current authorities, and existing reconciliation records.
reconcile-knowledge.outputs: A comparison and, when authorized, verified reversible dispositions.
reconcile-knowledge.example: Compare these two project folders and identify unique material before proposing any moves.
reconcile-knowledge.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
reconcile-knowledge.expect: It starts from one named folder and the comparison roots, hashes only changed files, and classifies each as duplicate, divergent, complementary, unique or unresolved. It archives only verified duplicates with a reversible move manifest, never deletes permanently, and stops at a plan for a comparison-only request.
reconcile-knowledge.requires: The named folder and comparison roots mounted and readable, and a configured knowledge hub connection.
reconcile-knowledge.overview: It starts from one named folder and the comparison roots, hashes only changed files, and classifies each as duplicate, divergent, complementary, unique or unresolved. It archives only verified duplicates with a reversible move manifest, never deletes permanently, and stops at a plan for a comparison-only request.
reconcile-knowledge.value: Separate exact duplicates from complementary or conflicting files before cleanup. It helps preserve the version that matters and makes any authorized archive move traceable and reversible.

preparation.where: Name the folder being reviewed and the folders or records it should be compared with. Current authorities are the documents your project treats as controlling; point to them or explain who owns that decision.
preparation.missing: If a folder is unavailable or authority is unresolved, that comparison remains open. Start with a comparison plan; no move follows merely from similar names, age or location.

manage-linked-task.what: Connect a Codex work item to the user’s Brain task record.
manage-linked-task.when: Starting, continuing, or completing a Brain-linked task.
manage-linked-task.inputs: The task ID, current Brain note, and access to the task bridge.
manage-linked-task.outputs: The task’s supported state, work receipt, and linked chat where applicable.
manage-linked-task.example: Continue this Brain task and record the result when its acceptance checks pass.
manage-linked-task.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
manage-linked-task.expect: It sets a linked task to in-progress, finds or creates its working chat through the task bridge, and records a receipt with specific verification at a work boundary. An idle or archived chat never closes a task, and it creates a chat only when that is explicitly authorized.
manage-linked-task.requires: A configured task vault with its task helper and bridge scripts, python3, and the Codex app for creating linked chats.
manage-linked-task.overview: It sets a linked task to in-progress, finds or creates its working chat through the task bridge, and records a receipt with specific verification at a work boundary. An idle or archived chat never closes a task, and it creates a chat only when that is explicitly authorized.
manage-linked-task.value: Keep the actual work, its chat and its task record connected. It is useful when a task must remain open until its requested result and verification have been recorded, even if the chat is idle.

preparation.where: Supply the task ID and access to the task vault. The task bridge is an existing helper script connecting the vault to Codex; its location and configuration come from your installation.
preparation.missing: Without the configured vault or bridge, the linked-task operation cannot run. You can discuss the task, but its external status must not be reported as updated. Creating another chat also needs your instruction.

brand-renderer.what: Render an artifact using the selected visual identity.
brand-renderer.when: A document, deck, workbook, PDF, or page needs branded rendering.
brand-renderer.inputs: The artifact, confirmed brand profile or neutral defaults, and rendering runtime.
brand-renderer.outputs: Rendered files, brand checks, and findings from visual inspection.
brand-renderer.example: Render this report using the confirmed project brand and inspect the exported pages.
brand-renderer.expect: It resolves the selected brand profile (or the neutral policy), proves its runtime with a preflight, then runs parity, visual, prose and brand gates on the rendered artifact. A selected profile that is missing or invalid is an error, and a release needs a written disposition for every warning.
brand-renderer.overview: It takes content from a producing workflow, resolves the selected brand profile or neutral defaults, checks that the format's runtime is available and renders the artifact. It then compares the output with the source content and performs visual, writing and brand checks. It supports documents, decks, workbooks, PDFs and pages through the relevant format tools.
brand-renderer.value: Turn content into a checked document, deck, workbook or page using one selected identity. It is the rendering helper that keeps layout, brand values and exported content consistent across producing skills.

preparation.where: The calling workflow supplies the content, output format and confirmed brand profile. A profile records colors, fonts and permitted assets; neutral defaults are available when no identity is selected. Rendering tools are format-specific runtime dependencies.
preparation.missing: An explicitly selected missing or invalid profile must be supplied or corrected. Without the required renderer, an export cannot be verified. This helper is included in the complete packages that declare it; you normally use the producing skill.

build-interactive-explorer.what: Build an interactive website with project-specific navigation, expandable details and source references.
build-interactive-explorer.when: Source material needs a clickable explanation such as a solution explorer, research hub, process guide or journey view.
build-interactive-explorer.inputs: The topic, its sources, and the intended audience and destination.
build-interactive-explorer.outputs: A website organized around the audience and source material, with optional validated roadmap snapshots.
build-interactive-explorer.example: Turn these discovery notes into an interactive explorer with seller and enterprise paths and a delivery roadmap.
build-interactive-explorer.expect: It reads the sources, chooses a structure for the reader’s task, and builds through the available site workflow. Paths appear when the material has distinct routes. Claims retain their evidence, and publishing stays private unless a wider audience is approved. Material deliverables receive writing-integrity, visual and web-app interaction assessments; source facts, working behavior and user design acceptance remain distinct.
build-interactive-explorer.requires: A supported website implementation workflow and the dependencies needed by the chosen project. Optional roadmaps use the bundled roadmap tooling.
build-interactive-explorer.overview: It turns source material into a website whose structure fits the reader’s task and the relationship being explained. Readers can compare findings, browse themes or follow a meaningful sequence, with supporting evidence beside the claims. Visual design follows the project profile rather than a fixed shell.
build-interactive-explorer.value: Help readers find the relevant explanation and inspect its evidence without reading every source document in full.

preparation.where: Provide source documents or notes, the intended readers, their questions and the desired destination. Include an existing project brand or design reference when one governs the work.
preparation.missing: Choose a useful structure from the available material and identify important gaps. Omit unsupported content. If publication tools are unavailable, deliver the local website and explain what remains.

write-business-case.what: Write the business case a funding approver reads, including the case against and the cost of waiting.
write-business-case.when: An approver needs to decide whether to fund an initiative.
write-business-case.inputs: A validated evidence ledger, the quote for engagement costs, sourced client value figures and the dated events that drive timing.
write-business-case.outputs: A gated business case with sourced figures, shown cost-of-delay arithmetic, sourced risks and a bounded ask, or a readiness gap memo when evidence is insufficient.
write-business-case.example: Build the business case for this initiative from the quote, the discovery findings and the renewal date.
write-business-case.expect: It builds an evidence ledger first and stops with a readiness gap memo if a load-bearing area is insufficient. The draft must include a case against, shown arithmetic and source tokens on every figure, and a structural gate checks these before release.
write-business-case.requires: Needs the evidence-core skill, a quote or user-supplied pricing source for cost figures, and python3 to run the case gate.
write-business-case.overview: It builds an evidence ledger from your sources, checks whether the central cost and benefit claims have enough support, and develops the investment argument: benefits, costs, alternatives, risks, the case against and the cost of waiting. Figures carry their sources and calculations. If the evidence is insufficient, it returns a readiness-gap memo instead of a full funding case.
write-business-case.value: Help an approver decide whether an initiative merits investment. It brings benefits, costs, alternatives, risks and the cost of waiting into one argument, including reasons the investment might not be justified.

preparation.where: Bring discovery findings, a quote or other cost source, benefit evidence and relevant deadlines. An evidence ledger is a source-and-claim register; Evidence core prepares it from the project material. It is a helper in the complete package, not a document you must already have written.
preparation.missing: The workflow can begin by assessing your sources. If a central benefit, cost or timing claim lacks enough support, it returns a readiness-gap memo rather than a persuasive-looking business case built on guesses.

preparationSkills.reason: Creates and checks the source-and-claim ledger before drafting the investment case.

prepare-sales-pursuit.what: Prepare a pursuit or an upcoming sales conversation.
prepare-sales-pursuit.when: A pursuit brief, call objective, agenda, or stakeholder plan is needed.
prepare-sales-pursuit.inputs: Account evidence, attendees, pursuit context, and the upcoming decision.
prepare-sales-pursuit.outputs: A pursuit or call brief with ranked questions and recommended next steps.
prepare-sales-pursuit.example: Prepare a call brief for this account with an objective, agenda, and ranked questions.
prepare-sales-pursuit.expect: It works in one of two modes: it maintains a Pursuit Brief for the opportunity or prepares one upcoming call from the calendar invite and attendee list. Every claim carries a source, inferences are labeled, figures are reconciled before use, and gaps are reported in chat rather than in the document.
prepare-sales-pursuit.requires: Needs the pursuit sources or client profile, the invite or attendee list for a call, and python3 to run the brief checks.
prepare-sales-pursuit.overview: It works in one of two modes: it maintains a Pursuit Brief for the opportunity or prepares one upcoming call from the calendar invite and attendee list. Every claim carries a source, inferences are labeled, figures are reconciled before use, and gaps are reported in chat rather than in the document.
prepare-sales-pursuit.value: Make the next sales conversation purposeful. It turns account evidence into a call objective, agenda, stakeholder approach and ranked questions, or maintains a longer pursuit brief as the opportunity develops.

preparation.where: Provide an account or opportunity name and the sources you have: CRM export, client notes, RFP, prior calls or a client profile. For a specific call, include the invite, attendees and decision you want to advance. A client profile is background information, not a required separate skill.
preparation.missing: Start with the available sources and mark unknowns. Without evidence for an account claim it remains an inference or question. Missing figures are not supplied from memory; the skill does not estimate a price for the pursuit.

prepare-job-application.what: Prepare the user’s application and interview work for a selected role.
prepare-job-application.when: Assessing a posting, tailoring materials, or preparing an interview.
prepare-job-application.inputs: The current posting, the user’s career sources, and the role work record.
prepare-job-application.outputs: Role assessment, tailored materials, interview preparation, or authorized form work.
prepare-job-application.example: Assess this posting against my current career direction and prepare the selected application materials.
prepare-job-application.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
prepare-job-application.expect: It reads the current posting, career authorities and role record, then selects evidence for that application. It checks role fit, career accuracy and evidence selection without requiring a people, practice or client theme. Form work retains its existing authorization and confirmation boundaries.
prepare-job-application.requires: The candidate's career evidence records (operating context, role work record, base resume), the live posting, and python3 for the readiness checker.
prepare-job-application.overview: It reads the current posting, career authorities and role record, then selects evidence for that application. It checks role fit, career accuracy and evidence selection without requiring a people, practice or client theme. Form work retains its existing authorization and confirmation boundaries.
prepare-job-application.value: Select supported experience for the actual hiring mandate while keeping career facts and application state consistent.

preparation.where: Supply the posting, your resume, career evidence and preferences. A role work record is the working file for this application: role requirements, evidence matches and decisions. The operating context is your career goals and constraints, supplied as notes or an existing record.
preparation.missing: If those records are absent, identify what evidence and decisions must be assembled first; a general resume alone may not support tailored claims. Form answers involving salary, authorization, attestations or submission still require your input.

preparationSkills.reason: Drafts supporting pieces after the role evidence has been mapped.
Applies the resume wording method to the selected role.

draft-application-materials.what: Draft supporting application materials in the user’s voice.
draft-application-materials.when: A cover letter, form answer, outreach draft, or LinkedIn section is needed.
draft-application-materials.inputs: The role record, current career evidence, and the requested audience.
draft-application-materials.outputs: Complete drafts tied to the role and the user’s supported experience.
draft-application-materials.example: Draft a cover letter for this role from my current role work record.
draft-application-materials.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
draft-application-materials.expect: It drafts each requested letter, form answer or supporting piece for its question and audience. Facts stay consistent with the résumé, while the examples may differ. It uses corrected claim authority and preserves the existing boundaries for private material, sensitive form answers, sending and publication.
draft-application-materials.requires: The candidate's role work record, tailored resume, live posting, professional profile and a confirmed author profile.
draft-application-materials.overview: It drafts each requested letter, form answer or supporting piece for its question and audience. Facts stay consistent with the résumé, while the examples may differ. It uses corrected claim authority and preserves the existing boundaries for private material, sensitive form answers, sending and publication.
draft-application-materials.value: Give each application surface useful supported content rather than repeating the résumé’s examples or a standing differentiator.

preparation.where: Use the role's work record, tailored resume and posting. The translation table connects the employer's requirements to your experience; it belongs in that role record. A writing profile is an optional separately authorized source of voice preferences, not permission to read private messages.
preparation.missing: For the full application workflow, prepare the role translation table through Prepare job application or supply an equivalent mapping. For a short bounded draft, you can provide relevant facts inline; missing optional records limit claims rather than forcing an outline. Salary and work-authorization questions still need your answer.

preparationSkills.reason: Prepares the role record and evidence translation for a full application.

assess-career-options.what: Compare roles and offers against the candidate’s chosen career direction.
assess-career-options.when: A role screen, tracker review, negotiation, or offer comparison.
assess-career-options.inputs: Role or offer terms, the user’s criteria, and the current career record.
assess-career-options.outputs: A comparison, open questions, and negotiation drafts for the user’s decision.
assess-career-options.example: Compare these offers against my recorded career gates and list the unresolved terms.
assess-career-options.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
assess-career-options.expect: It compares the actual opportunity with the candidate’s current pay, scope, billability and progression criteria. Unknown terms remain questions. It does not infer a permanent market identity or downgrade an opportunity merely because its category differs from earlier applications.
assess-career-options.requires: The candidate's operating context, tracker, role work record, pay thresholds and the posting or written offer.
assess-career-options.overview: It compares the actual opportunity with the candidate’s current pay, scope, billability and progression criteria. Unknown terms remain questions. It does not infer a permanent market identity or downgrade an opportunity merely because its category differs from earlier applications.
assess-career-options.value: Assess opportunities against the criteria the candidate chose, with role facts and uncertainties visible.

preparation.where: Provide the posting or written offer and your criteria, including pay thresholds and any weights. Your tracker and role record are your own records of opportunities and evidence; supplied files can explain those terms without adopting someone else's career goals.
preparation.missing: Missing thresholds or weights require your decision. Unknown offer terms remain questions for the employer; a negotiation figure is not invented. The skill prepares the comparison and draft wording, while you choose the offer.

write-portfolio-case-study.what: Turn the user’s work into a portfolio case study.
write-portfolio-case-study.when: A project or engagement needs a case study for the user’s portfolio.
write-portfolio-case-study.inputs: Project evidence, the user’s template, and current claims and rights decisions.
write-portfolio-case-study.outputs: A working copy and a clean publish copy with unresolved gaps kept in the working record.
write-portfolio-case-study.example: Turn this project into a working case study and publish copy using my claims ledger.
write-portfolio-case-study.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
write-portfolio-case-study.expect: It produces two copies each time: a working copy with evidence labels on every figure and a clean publish copy in first person. It brackets missing facts instead of filling them and checks six publish gates, including sanitization and ownership, before anything is called ready.
write-portfolio-case-study.requires: The candidate's publication rights ledger, program records and evidence ledger, and a confirmed author profile.
write-portfolio-case-study.overview: It produces two copies each time: a working copy with evidence labels on every figure and a clean publish copy in first person. It brackets missing facts instead of filling them and checks six publish gates, including sanitization and ownership, before anything is called ready.
write-portfolio-case-study.value: Explain the problem, your contribution and what the work made possible in a portfolio-ready story. It separates the evidence-heavy working copy from the copy a prospective client or employer should read.

preparation.where: Bring project artifacts, your role and contribution, outcomes and the intended case-study format. A claims-and-rights ledger records which statements, names, images and client details may be published; it comes from your project or career records.
preparation.missing: Missing facts are bracketed in the working copy. If ownership or publication rights are unresolved, those gates remain open; the skill cannot infer permission from possession of a document. A style profile must be authorized for this use.

preparationSkills.reason: Uses your authorized profile when you want writing in a confirmed personal voice.

manage-brand-profile.what: Apply the confirmed project or client identity.
manage-brand-profile.when: An artifact needs a brand profile or existing profile applied.
manage-brand-profile.inputs: The project’s confirmed colors, typography, assets, and usage rights.
manage-brand-profile.outputs: A selected or updated profile and an artifact checked against it.
manage-brand-profile.example: Apply this confirmed brand profile to the document and check the rendered result.
manage-brand-profile.expect: It chooses the brand from your explicit choice or the project's brand file, falling back to the neutral profile, and says which one governs. It marks a new profile as draft until you confirm it and checks the output for mixed identities.
manage-brand-profile.overview: It chooses the brand from your explicit choice or the project's brand file, falling back to the neutral profile, and says which one governs. It marks a new profile as draft until you confirm it and checks the output for mixed identities.
manage-brand-profile.value: Apply one consistent visual identity to an artifact, or turn a supplied brand guide into a profile that future work can use. It helps prevent mixed client identities and guessed colors or logos.

preparation.where: Provide a confirmed brand.md file or the brand guide and authorized logo/font assets. A brand profile is that record of exact values and usage rights; it is not an account connection. Select a brand explicitly when more than one could apply.
preparation.missing: With no confirmed brand selected, use the neutral profile. A newly extracted profile stays draft until confirmed; a missing logo is not redrawn or invented. You can begin with the neutral identity without creating a custom profile.

simplify-code.what: Simplify the current code change for reuse, clarity, maintainability and efficiency without changing behavior.
simplify-code.when: A delivery workflow names a simplify pass, or a non-trivial diff needs cleanup before commit.
simplify-code.inputs: The current branch diff or an explicit target, repository conventions and the relevant tests.
simplify-code.outputs: High-confidence refinements with test evidence, plus behavior-changing candidates reported separately instead of applied.
simplify-code.example: Review this diff for duplication and unnecessary complexity while preserving its behavior.
simplify-code.expect: It works on the current branch diff or a target you name, reads the surrounding code and tests, and applies only high-confidence edits for reuse, clarity, maintainability and efficiency. It preserves behavior, stops if the diff base is ambiguous, and reports cleanups that would change behavior as recommendations rather than applying them.
simplify-code.requires: A git repository containing the change, and the project's formatter, static checks and tests.
simplify-code.overview: It works on the current branch diff or a target you name, reads the surrounding code and tests, and applies only high-confidence edits for reuse, clarity, maintainability and efficiency. It preserves behavior, stops if the diff base is ambiguous, and reports cleanups that would change behavior as recommendations rather than applying them.
simplify-code.value: Remove duplication and unnecessary complexity from an existing change while preserving its behavior. It helps make a diff easier to review and maintain without expanding the feature being delivered.

preparation.where: Point to the branch diff or specific code to simplify, its surrounding implementation and the repository's checks. Project conventions usually live in its README, contributor instructions, formatting configuration and nearby code.
preparation.missing: An ambiguous diff base must be resolved before editing. Missing tests limit the behavior evidence; changes that would alter behavior are recommendations rather than silently applied cleanup.

release-skill-package.what: Package a skill for Codex and Claude destinations.
release-skill-package.when: A shared skill needs packaging, replacement, or destination inspection.
release-skill-package.inputs: The source package, target hosts, and supported installation or upload path.
release-skill-package.outputs: A portable release package and separately verified destination states.
release-skill-package.example: Package this reviewed skill for the specified Codex and Claude destinations.
release-skill-package.expect: It identifies the skill, source and requested destinations, builds the package, and inspects the archive hash and contents before installing or replacing anything. It stops at the destinations you requested, keeps a private replacement private, and reports an upload and a verified invocation as separate states.
release-skill-package.overview: It identifies the skill, source and requested destinations, builds the package, and inspects the archive hash and contents before installing or replacing anything. It stops at the destinations you requested, keeps a private replacement private, and reports an upload and a verified invocation as separate states.
release-skill-package.value: Move a reviewed skill to the requested assistant or account with its scripts and references intact. It checks the archive and destination separately so a successful ZIP build is not mistaken for an installed, working skill.

preparation.where: Supply the skill source, intended hosts and requested operation: package, install, replace or inspect. Destination installation rules come from that host's current supported method; the skill does not provide accounts or access.
preparation.missing: If a destination or upload method is unavailable, stop at the verified local package and report the remaining operation. This is a maintenance mode included in Maintain skills estate; another host is not updated merely because the package exists.

preparationSkills.reason: Owns the package containing this cross-host release mode.

manage-cutover-closeout.what: Prepare cutover, hypercare, and delivery closeout.
manage-cutover-closeout.when: An accepted release is approaching go-live or closeout.
manage-cutover-closeout.inputs: Executed scope, release evidence, owners, and the go or no-go decision.
manage-cutover-closeout.outputs: A cutover runbook, acceptance record, hypercare plan, and closeout materials.
manage-cutover-closeout.example: Prepare the cutover runbook and hypercare plan from this accepted release.
manage-cutover-closeout.expect: It builds the cutover runbook, the Go-Live Acceptance tracker, hypercare triage and the closeout record from the executed SOW and the signed readiness pack. It will not plan production cutover without the go decision, will not invent an acceptance deadline the SOW does not support, and leaves acceptance, rollback and closeout approvals to humans.
manage-cutover-closeout.requires: Needs an approved go or no-go decision, the executed SOW, and python3 to run the closeout gate.
manage-cutover-closeout.overview: It builds the cutover runbook, the Go-Live Acceptance tracker, hypercare triage and the closeout record from the executed SOW and the signed readiness pack. It will not plan production cutover without the go decision, will not invent an acceptance deadline the SOW does not support, and leaves acceptance, rollback and closeout approvals to humans.
manage-cutover-closeout.value: Organize the transition from an accepted release to go-live, support and formal closeout. It makes responsibilities, acceptance evidence and rollback decisions inspectable when the cost of a missed handoff is high.

preparation.where: Use the signed statement of work, approved readiness pack, named owners and go/no-go decision. These come from the engagement's delivery records; Validate delivery prepares the testing/readiness evidence. Hypercare means the defined support period after go-live.
preparation.missing: Without the go decision it does not plan production cutover as approved. Missing contractual acceptance terms must be resolved with the agreement owner; dates and sign-offs are not inferred from a template.

preparationSkills.reason: Prepares the testing and readiness evidence required for the go/no-go decision.

build-deal-decision-deck.what: Build a deck for a scope or proposal decision.
build-deal-decision-deck.when: A buyer needs to compare options or confirm one proposal direction.
build-deal-decision-deck.inputs: Scoped options, supporting evidence, commercial inputs, and the decision mode.
build-deal-decision-deck.outputs: A reviewed decision narrative and editable presentation.
build-deal-decision-deck.example: Build a decision deck comparing these two scoped options for the buyer.
build-deal-decision-deck.expect: It pins the mode (decision or confirmation), audience and quote source, builds a manifest, and gates it with a no-render check before any slide-by-slide copy approval. It refuses to render on a preflight failure or an unresolved flag, and on an unattended run it stops before approvals instead of simulating them.
build-deal-decision-deck.requires: Needs a quote identifier with its source data, Node for the gate, pptxgenjs to render the PPTX, and python-pptx to extract an existing deck.
build-deal-decision-deck.overview: It pins the mode (decision or confirmation), audience and quote source, builds a manifest, and gates it with a no-render check before any slide-by-slide copy approval. It refuses to render on a preflight failure or an unresolved flag, and on an unattended run it stops before approvals instead of simulating them.
build-deal-decision-deck.value: Help a buyer compare scoped options or confirm a selected proposal direction. It puts the decision and commercial implications ahead of a generic sales story.

preparation.where: Bring the quote export or pricing source, scoped options, audience and decision to make. A manifest is the structured outline and figures the skill prepares before rendering. It is not a presentation you must build first.
preparation.missing: A missing or inconsistent quote source blocks a priced decision deck. It can identify the missing inputs, but unresolved flags and copy approvals cannot be simulated. Rendering requires the documented presentation runtime.

review-deal-economics.what: Prepare the internal Deal Desk packet that shows a deal's computed margin against the approval policy.
review-deal-economics.when: A priced quote needs internal commercial approval before proposal or SOW, or a packet's figures need tie-out.
review-deal-economics.inputs: The quote, the confirmed margin floor and approval ladder, the evidence ledger and the delivery lead's cosign answer.
review-deal-economics.outputs: A gated packet with recomputed margin, flagged risks, routed asks, an empty decisions log and a figure tie-out against the quote.
review-deal-economics.example: Prepare the Deal Desk packet for this quote and tie out the SOW draft's figures against it.
review-deal-economics.expect: It orients on the quote, confirms the margin floor and approval ladder, then builds a readout with margin as the headline and every flag visible. It asks for the delivery cosign rather than inferring it, recomputes margin in a gate, and never adjusts hours or rates to rescue a number.
review-deal-economics.requires: Needs a priced quote (Q-number) or export, the project's margin floor and approval policy, and python3 to run the gate and tie-out.
review-deal-economics.overview: It orients on the quote, confirms the margin floor and approval ladder, then builds a readout with margin as the headline and every flag visible. It asks for the delivery cosign rather than inferring it, recomputes margin in a gate, and never adjusts hours or rates to rescue a number.
review-deal-economics.value: Show whether a priced deal meets the organization's commercial approval policy and which exceptions need a decision. It recomputes margin and ties document figures back to the quote rather than adjusting assumptions to make a deal pass.

preparation.where: Provide a priced quote or export, the margin floor, approval ladder and delivery lead's actual cosign. The floor and ladder are your organization's thresholds and approvers, usually held in commercial policy or supplied by its owner.
preparation.missing: No universal margin threshold is assumed. Missing policy or cosign remains an approval gap. A quote number alone is insufficient without its figures; a connected quoting system is optional when an export is supplied.

build-deck.what: Build a presentation around the audience’s decision.
build-deck.when: A pitch, proposal, reading deck, or technical briefing is needed.
build-deck.inputs: The audience, decision, source evidence, and output requirements.
build-deck.outputs: An editable deck with reviewed copy, explanatory visuals, and rendered checks.
build-deck.example: Create a briefing deck that helps this audience decide between the supported options.
build-deck.expect: It saves a brief, one-sentence thesis, submessages, slide structure and copy as separate records, in that order, before building anything. The thesis must pass a gate before slides are planned, and a QA pass over the finished deck is written up as a polish list.
build-deck.requires: Needs an engagement folder with a brief (audience and decision), python3 for the HTML build, and a presentation tool for PowerPoint output.
build-deck.overview: It develops the presentation's argument before drawing slides: audience and decision, a one-sentence thesis, supporting messages, slide structure and complete copy. It then builds the editable presentation with explanatory visuals and reviews the rendered result. The thesis is checked before slide planning, and remaining visual repairs are recorded in a polish list.
build-deck.value: Turn evidence into a presentation that helps a particular audience make a decision. It develops the argument before slide layouts, so the deck has a purpose beyond collecting information on slides.

preparation.where: Provide the audience, decision, sources and desired format. The brief can begin as your request; thesis and slide-plan records are working files the skill creates. PowerPoint output needs a presentation tool, while the documented HTML path uses its local build tools.
preparation.missing: If a decision or supporting claim is unresolved, settle it before treating the slide story as final. A missing renderer prevents that export; approving a narrative is separate from inspecting finished slides.

start-delivery.what: Mobilize a signed engagement from the accepted handoff and the signed SOW.
start-delivery.when: The sales-to-delivery handoff is accepted and kickoff is next.
start-delivery.inputs: The accepted handoff brief, the signed SOW, the confirmed delivery model and the shared engagement record.
start-delivery.outputs: A gated draft charter, seeded RAID and decision logs, internal and client kickoff decks, and a Sprint 0 or mobilization plan.
start-delivery.example: Prepare the charter, governance logs and kickoff decks from the signed SOW and the accepted handoff.
start-delivery.expect: It starts from the accepted handoff brief and signed SOW and drafts the charter, RAID and decision logs, kickoff decks and Sprint 0 plan. It stops if no accepted handoff exists, restates SOW scope without renegotiating it, and drafts what humans sign without signing or provisioning anything.
start-delivery.requires: Needs an accepted sales-to-delivery handoff brief, the signed SOW, and python3 to run the charter check.
start-delivery.overview: It starts from the accepted handoff brief and signed SOW and drafts the charter, RAID and decision logs, kickoff decks and Sprint 0 plan. It stops if no accepted handoff exists, restates SOW scope without renegotiating it, and drafts what humans sign without signing or provisioning anything.
start-delivery.value: Give the delivery team a common starting point after a sale: agreed scope, governance, responsibilities, kickoff materials and the first mobilization plan. It reduces the chance that sales assumptions become unexamined delivery commitments.

preparation.where: Supply the signed SOW and accepted sales-to-delivery handoff from the engagement record. The charter records delivery purpose, scope and governance. RAID means risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies; those logs are seeded during this workflow.
preparation.missing: An accepted handoff is required. If it does not exist, use Prepare delivery handoff and obtain the receiving owner's acceptance first. The skill drafts the charter and kickoff material but cannot sign them or provision project access for you.

preparationSkills.reason: Prepares the handoff that the receiving delivery owner must accept before kickoff.

track-delivery.what: Issue the period's delivery status, steward the RAID and decision logs, and check work against the SOW scope.
track-delivery.when: A weekly status report, a decision or risk to log, or a check of whether a request is in scope.
track-delivery.inputs: The period's transcripts, the RAID and decision logs, the SOW scope baseline, the previous status file and a timesheet or quote for burn.
track-delivery.outputs: A gated status report, append-only log entries with stable IDs, and change-order candidates with an evidence trail.
track-delivery.example: Write this week's status from the transcripts and logs, and flag anything that looks outside the SOW.
track-delivery.expect: It pins the engagement, the exact period and the previous status file, then reads the period's transcripts and updates the RAID and decision logs with stable IDs. It flags scope drift as a change-order candidate with quoted evidence, shows burn only from a named source, and a blocking gate must pass before the report is issued.
track-delivery.requires: Needs the RAID and decision logs from kickoff, the SOW scope baseline, the period's transcripts, and python3 to run the status gate.
track-delivery.overview: It pins the engagement, the exact period and the previous status file, then reads the period's transcripts and updates the RAID and decision logs with stable IDs. It flags scope drift as a change-order candidate with quoted evidence, shows burn only from a named source, and a blocking gate must pass before the report is issued.
track-delivery.value: Explain what changed during a reporting period, what threatens delivery and which requests may exceed agreed scope. It connects the status narrative to the same risk and decision records the team uses to act.

preparation.where: Provide the reporting period, previous status, meeting notes, executed SOW and RAID/decision logs. The SOW is the signed scope baseline; the logs normally come from kickoff. Burn figures need an actual timesheet, financial export or named quote source.
preparation.missing: Missing source figures remain unavailable rather than estimated as actual burn. Without a scope baseline, a request cannot be confidently classified as a scope change; the output must retain that gap and the relevant owner.

delivery-orchestrator.what: Route delivery work to the appropriate stage and owner.
delivery-orchestrator.when: A signed engagement needs coordination across delivery stages.
delivery-orchestrator.inputs: Executed scope, current delivery state, and the requested decision.
delivery-orchestrator.outputs: An updated stage record and the next owning workflow or gate.
delivery-orchestrator.example: Review this engagement’s delivery state and route the next work to its owner.
delivery-orchestrator.expect: It reads the engagement's DELIVERY-STATE.md, runs the planner to find the current stage and the next gate, and hands the work to the skill that owns it by name. It builds no artifacts itself, never marks a gate passed without its signed record, and does not touch pre-signature work.
delivery-orchestrator.requires: Needs the engagement's DELIVERY-STATE.md (or the delivery records needed to write one) and python3 to run the planner.
delivery-orchestrator.overview: It reads the engagement's DELIVERY-STATE.md, runs the planner to find the current stage and the next gate, and hands the work to the skill that owns it by name. It builds no artifacts itself, never marks a gate passed without its signed record, and does not touch pre-signature work.
delivery-orchestrator.value: Identify the next delivery stage and the person or workflow that owns its gate. It is useful when a signed engagement has many interdependent deliverables and the next step is unclear.

preparation.where: Supply the signed engagement's records and DELIVERY-STATE.md, the stage-and-gate record read by its planner. If the file does not exist, the workflow accepts records of completed stages so a state record can be written.
preparation.missing: Missing sign-offs cannot be replaced with an assumed stage. It routes to a producing skill rather than making every artifact itself; it does not cover pre-signature sales work.

preparationSkills.reason: Owns kickoff artifacts when the recorded delivery state reaches mobilization.

maintain-discovery-record.what: Maintain the findings and open questions for a pursuit.
maintain-discovery-record.when: Preparing discovery or incorporating a completed call.
maintain-discovery-record.inputs: The pursuit record, source notes, and scope or pricing questions.
maintain-discovery-record.outputs: A sourced discovery ledger and ranked questions that unblock the pursuit.
maintain-discovery-record.example: Update the pursuit ledger from this call and rank the unanswered scope questions.
maintain-discovery-record.expect: It builds a two-column ledger of supported facts and ranked open questions tied to the scope each one unblocks, before and after a discovery session. A transcript is ingested to close questions only with evidence, a priced unresolved item fails the brief, and it never creates hours, rates or fees.
maintain-discovery-record.requires: Needs the pursuit's sources (RFP, CRM record, transcripts, client documents) and python3 to run the ledger check.
maintain-discovery-record.overview: It builds a two-column ledger of supported facts and ranked open questions tied to the scope each one unblocks, before and after a discovery session. A transcript is ingested to close questions only with evidence, a priced unresolved item fails the brief, and it never creates hours, rates or fees.
maintain-discovery-record.value: Keep a pursuit's known facts and open questions connected to scope decisions. After a call, it shows which uncertainty was resolved and which question should be asked next to unblock an estimate or proposal.

preparation.where: Bring the pursuit identity, current ledger if one exists, and notes, transcripts, RFP or CRM exports. The ledger is a two-column working record of supported findings and ranked questions, not a prerequisite database product.
preparation.missing: It can build the ledger from the supplied sources. Unanswered questions remain open; unresolved scope must not acquire a price or estimate simply to complete the brief. A prior ledger is helpful but not the source of invented facts.

synthesize-discovery.what: Turn discovery calls and interview notes into sourced research findings.
synthesize-discovery.when: Supplied meeting content needs synthesis into what was learned.
synthesize-discovery.inputs: Transcripts or notes, the attendees on each side and the research purpose.
synthesize-discovery.outputs: A TL;DR, job statements, pain points with severity, exact quotes, speaker insights, open questions and named gaps.
synthesize-discovery.example: Synthesize these three discovery calls into findings, pain points and exact quotes with speakers.
synthesize-discovery.expect: It first confirms the client, meeting type and who attended, then reads the whole transcript or notes and separates client voices from the consulting team's. It quotes only words present in the source, rates severity from the source wording, and will not call the result final until the writing review and quality gate have passed.
synthesize-discovery.requires: Needs the call content itself (pasted notes, a text, Word or PDF file, or a Granola transcript through its connector) and a confirmed client and project context; audio files are not accepted.
synthesize-discovery.overview: It first confirms the client, meeting type and who attended, then reads the whole transcript or notes and separates client voices from the consulting team's. It quotes only words present in the source, rates severity from the source wording, and will not call the result final until the writing review and quality gate have passed.
synthesize-discovery.value: Extract what was learned from conversations: customer problems, jobs, severity, exact quotes and unanswered questions. It preserves who said what so a consultant's suggestion is not presented as a customer's requirement.

preparation.where: Provide the actual notes or transcript and identify the client, meeting purpose and attendees. Pasted text, supported documents or an available transcript connector can supply the content; no meeting connector is required when you provide a file.
preparation.missing: Audio is not an accepted substitute for a transcript in this workflow. Missing speaker or client context must be clarified. With no call content, it can help identify what to collect but cannot produce research findings or quotations.

promote-salesforce-changes.what: Prepare and perform an authorized DevOps Center promotion.
promote-salesforce-changes.when: Work items or a pipeline stage need promotion.
promote-salesforce-changes.inputs: The configured integration, target stage, work items, and authorization.
promote-salesforce-changes.outputs: Capability and dependency checks, promotion results, and unresolved conflicts.
promote-salesforce-changes.example: Check whether these work items are ready for promotion to the specified stage.
promote-salesforce-changes.expect: It runs a local capability check first, then verifies the confirmed target org and always runs promotion validation before anything is changed. It stops at a failed check, a missing org or a missing plugin capability instead of guessing, and does not claim a deployment succeeded from a started command.
promote-salesforce-changes.overview: It runs a local capability check first, then verifies the confirmed target org and always runs promotion validation before anything is changed. It stops at a failed check, a missing org or a missing plugin capability instead of guessing, and does not claim a deployment succeeded from a started command.
promote-salesforce-changes.value: Check whether selected DevOps Center work items can move to a target pipeline stage, then perform only the authorized promotion. It surfaces dependency and validation failures before a release is attempted.

preparation.where: Provide the work-item or project identifiers, target stage and intended Salesforce org. The configured DevOps Center integration and login must already exist in the environment; they are tools/accounts, not another skill.
preparation.missing: A missing plugin capability, login, target org or failed validation stops promotion. You can request a readiness check first. A started command is not evidence that the target environment was updated.

manage-salesforce-devops.what: Manage DevOps Center work items and review requests.
manage-salesforce-devops.when: Creating, updating, committing, or reviewing a work item.
manage-salesforce-devops.inputs: The configured integration, selected work item, and requested operation.
manage-salesforce-devops.outputs: The verified work-item change, commit, or review request.
manage-salesforce-devops.example: Inspect this DevOps Center work item and prepare the requested field update.
manage-salesforce-devops.expect: It asks for the confirmed target org, the operation (list, create, update, commit or open a pull request) and the project or work item, then checks the DevOps Center plugin before changing anything. It stops if the plugin or the org login is missing and confirms a status change from the returned result.
manage-salesforce-devops.overview: It asks for the confirmed target org, the operation (list, create, update, commit or open a pull request) and the project or work item, then checks the DevOps Center plugin before changing anything. It stops if the plugin or the org login is missing and confirms a status change from the returned result.
manage-salesforce-devops.value: Handle DevOps Center work-item operations without conflating them with deployment. It can inspect or update the selected item, commit changes and prepare its review request while retaining the returned operation result.

preparation.where: Specify the operation, project or work item and confirmed org. It uses the installed DevOps Center plugin and the environment's existing Salesforce authentication. For moving changes between stages, use the promotion mode instead.
preparation.missing: Without the plugin or org login, live work-item operations cannot run. The skill will not infer a target from an alias or claim a status change that the service has not confirmed.

evidence-core.what: Track source records and the claims an artifact can support.
evidence-core.when: A material client artifact needs evidence review.
evidence-core.inputs: The project sources, revisions, authority rules, and proposed claims.
evidence-core.outputs: A source register, atomic claims, conflicts, and an evidence sufficiency decision.
evidence-core.example: Build a claim ledger for this report using these versioned sources.
evidence-core.expect: It builds a ledger of sources and atomic claims first, with an authority score, status and owner for anything unresolved, and the document comes after. If a load-bearing area has too little evidence it writes a short readiness-gap memo and stops instead of drafting the full artifact.
evidence-core.requires: Needs source files or exports for the engagement, a Knowledge Hub location for the evidence records, and Python 3 to run the ledger validator.
evidence-core.overview: It builds a ledger of sources and atomic claims first, with an authority score, status and owner for anything unresolved, and the document comes after. If a load-bearing area has too little evidence it writes a short readiness-gap memo and stops instead of drafting the full artifact.
evidence-core.value: Check which claims a project artifact can support before drafting it. The source register records authority, conflicts and missing evidence behind each important claim. This makes unsupported recommendations easier to identify before a document is written.

preparation.where: Supply project documents or exports and identify where the source register should live. An evidence ledger is a table of individual claims linked to exact sources; this workflow creates it. Knowledge Hub means your selected project storage, which may be a folder or another supported store.
preparation.missing: You do not need an existing ledger to begin. If a central area lacks enough evidence, it produces a readiness-gap memo identifying the missing material instead of allowing the dependent artifact to proceed as if complete.

verify-work-state.what: Verify what changed and where the result exists.
verify-work-state.when: Work changes files, repositories, deployments, installations, or cloud records.
verify-work-state.inputs: The intended result, affected destination, and available verification access.
verify-work-state.outputs: A precise completion state with evidence and the remaining action.
verify-work-state.example: Verify which parts of this release are local, merged, published, and installed.
verify-work-state.expect: It identifies the requested outcome, the authoritative source and the finish line before work starts, then checks the destination system when the work ends. It will not report a local draft, commit or API response as a later state such as merged or live, and ends with what changed, what was verified, what is unchanged and the next action.
verify-work-state.overview: It identifies the requested outcome, the authoritative source and the finish line before work starts, then checks the destination system when the work ends. It will not report a local draft, commit or API response as a later state such as merged or live, and ends with what changed, what was verified, what is unchanged and the next action.
verify-work-state.value: Determine what actually exists at the end of a task: a local file, remote commit, merged change, deployment or installed package. It prevents a successful intermediate command from being reported as the requested final result.

preparation.where: State the intended outcome and the destination that owns the result. Verification evidence comes from that destination: file bytes, GitHub state, deployment response, installed version or cloud-record readback. No special project document is required for an ordinary bounded check.
preparation.missing: Without destination access, verification stops at the layer that can be observed. It names the unavailable check and remaining action instead of promoting a local artifact to live or installed.

guide-fortunes-weave.what: Answer questions and maintain the user’s Fortune’s Weave planner.
guide-fortunes-weave.when: A question concerns the user’s current route, roster, or planner.
guide-fortunes-weave.inputs: The planner project location, current roster, route sources and live planner state.
guide-fortunes-weave.outputs: A sourced answer or an authorized, verified planner update.
guide-fortunes-weave.example: Check my current route and roster before recommending the next planner update.
guide-fortunes-weave.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
guide-fortunes-weave.expect: It reads the live roster and planner state before recommending a team or changing a build, and pulls only the researched section it needs. It will not state niche game mechanics from memory or treat a suggested team as a confirmed roster, and it asks for a roster export if it cannot reach the planner.
guide-fortunes-weave.requires: Needs the planner project location and its current roster, either readable through an available tool or supplied as an export.
guide-fortunes-weave.overview: It reads the live roster and planner state before recommending a team or changing a build, and pulls only the researched section it needs. It will not state niche game mechanics from memory or treat a suggested team as a confirmed roster, and it asks for a roster export if it cannot reach the planner.
guide-fortunes-weave.value: Answer planner and game questions from the user's actual roster, route and current build. It keeps a suggested team or researched mechanic separate from something the planner already records.

preparation.where: Provide the Fortune's Weave planner project location or an export of its current roster and route. The router is the project's index to those files; it is not a separate skill or a universal folder installed with this workflow.
preparation.missing: If the planner cannot be reached, supply a roster export. Without current roster information, recommendations must not be represented as a valid update to your existing team; niche mechanics still need source verification.

work-in-github-repository.what: Work with the user’s GitHub repositories.
work-in-github-repository.when: A repository needs inspection, a commit, a PR, or release work.
work-in-github-repository.inputs: The explicitly identified repository, intended account and authorized change.
work-in-github-repository.outputs: Verified repository changes and separate PR, merge, or deployment state.
work-in-github-repository.example: Review this specified repository change and prepare a pull request.
work-in-github-repository.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
work-in-github-repository.expect: It inspects the remote, branch and working tree, then checks that the GitHub CLI can reach the named host, owner and repository before acting. It reads back the remote commit or pull request after a push, and it does not bypass protected branches, reviews or environment approvals or ask for a token.
work-in-github-repository.requires: Needs Git and the GitHub CLI (gh) installed and logged in to the target host with access to the repository.
work-in-github-repository.overview: It inspects the remote, branch and working tree, then checks that the GitHub CLI can reach the named host, owner and repository before acting. It reads back the remote commit or pull request after a push, and it does not bypass protected branches, reviews or environment approvals or ask for a token.
work-in-github-repository.value: Carry an authorized repository change through the relevant Git and GitHub steps with evidence from the remote. It keeps branch work, pull requests, merges and deployment states distinct.

preparation.where: Identify the repository URL or owner/name, target host and requested change. Local work needs Git; remote operations use an authenticated GitHub CLI with permission to that repository. Authentication comes from your environment, not from this skill.
preparation.missing: If access is missing, remote operations stop with the specific error. A local checkout can still be inspected where available. Tokens should not be pasted into chat, and repository access does not grant access to a separate deployment service.

develop-independent-product.what: Develop the user’s independent work from supplied historical projects.
develop-independent-product.when: An employer-era artifact is being translated into an independent product or offer.
develop-independent-product.inputs: Authorized historical sources, a project brief, and claims and rights decisions.
develop-independent-product.outputs: A usable independent artifact or backlog with source and publication questions resolved where possible.
develop-independent-product.example: Translate these authorized historical materials into an independent offering brief.
develop-independent-product.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
develop-independent-product.expect: It first confirms the user's authority and the reuse scope from the task, then drafts a short migration map of the useful mechanism, its original dependencies and the independent form. It rebuilds examples with synthetic data, removes client details before anything leaves the private workspace, and treats publication as a separate decision.
develop-independent-product.requires: Needs the historical project material and a user-selected home for the independent product.
develop-independent-product.overview: It first confirms the user's authority and the reuse scope from the task, then drafts a short migration map of the useful mechanism, its original dependencies and the independent form. It rebuilds examples with synthetic data, removes client details before anything leaves the private workspace, and treats publication as a separate decision.
develop-independent-product.value: Extract a reusable product mechanism from historical work and rebuild it for an independent offering. It helps distinguish the useful method from employer dependencies, private client details and publication rights.

preparation.where: Supply the historical artifacts you are authorized to use and a home for the independent project. Rights decisions mean the reuse scope and publication permissions you actually hold; a document's presence on disk is not proof of those permissions.
preparation.missing: If reuse authority is unresolved, keep that question open before distributing derived material. Synthetic examples can replace private data where supported; missing source mechanisms cannot be filled with invented history.

design-information-architecture.what: Organize navigation, content labels, and site structure.
design-information-architecture.when: A website or product needs better findability.
design-information-architecture.inputs: The audience, content inventory, tasks, and current navigation.
design-information-architecture.outputs: A sitemap, taxonomy, navigation proposal, or structural review.
design-information-architecture.example: Reorganize this site’s navigation around the tasks visitors need to complete.
design-information-architecture.expect: It reads the current content inventory and navigation before proposing anything, then gives a sitemap or structure with reasons tied to the audience's tasks. It keeps existing URLs unless a change is authorized, and it labels the result provisional because only real card sorts or tree tests count as validation.
design-information-architecture.overview: It reads the current content inventory and navigation before proposing anything, then gives a sitemap or structure with reasons tied to the audience's tasks. It keeps existing URLs unless a change is authorized, and it labels the result provisional because only real card sorts or tree tests count as validation.
design-information-architecture.value: Organize a site around the tasks readers need to complete. It examines the content and navigation to propose clearer groupings, labels and routes, making information easier to find.

preparation.where: Provide the site's content list, current navigation or sitemap, audience and important tasks. A content inventory can be an export, a list of pages or accessible existing pages; a formal sitemap is not required before beginning.
