preparation.missing: If the implementation cannot be read, affected files and existing behavior remain unverified. It can define supported requirements, but unresolved design choices must stay open and planned tests must not be reported as executed.

plan-sprint.what: Plan one sprint against measured team capacity.
plan-sprint.when: A team is about to commit to a sprint, or sprints keep missing their goal.
plan-sprint.inputs: Team availability, the refine-backlog readiness report, the RAID log, recent velocity and the definition of done.
plan-sprint.outputs: A sprint plan with a goal, capacity, commit and stretch work, owned dependencies and a gate result.
plan-sprint.example: Plan sprint 5 for a team of four with one person out for three days.
plan-sprint.expect: It asks for capacity, velocity, the definition of done and the readiness report, then drafts a sprint goal and a commit and stretch split and runs a gate script. The gate exits 1 on over-capacity or not-ready commitments, and the plan is a proposal because the team decides the commitment and the tracker is never changed.
plan-sprint.requires: Python 3 for the gate script, plus a readiness report from backlog refinement and a RAID log if you want the gate to check them.
plan-sprint.overview: It asks for capacity, velocity, the definition of done and the readiness report, then drafts a sprint goal and a commit and stretch split and runs a gate script. The gate exits 1 on over-capacity or not-ready commitments, and the plan is a proposal because the team decides the commitment and the tracker is never changed.
plan-sprint.value: Match a proposed sprint commitment to actual availability and ready work. It makes capacity overruns, unresolved dependencies and stretch work visible before the team commits.

preparation.where: Bring team availability, recent velocity, a definition of done and the readiness report from Refine backlog. The RAID log lists risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies. Equivalent team records can explain these inputs; they are not supplied by connecting a tracker alone.
preparation.missing: Missing estimates or readiness evidence must be supplied by the team or prepared through refinement. The gate cannot approve over-capacity or not-ready commitments. The plan is a proposal; it does not change tracker tickets or choose the team's commitment.

preparationSkills.reason: Prepares the readiness report used to select a proposed commitment.

design-sticker.what: Develop and critique typography-led sticker designs.
design-sticker.when: A sticker concept needs composition, type exploration, or print-scale review.
design-sticker.inputs: The concept, collection references, source assets, and production constraints.
design-sticker.outputs: Design directions, refined compositions, and print-scale proofs.
design-sticker.example: Develop distinct type treatments for this sticker concept and review them at print scale.
design-sticker.expect: It works from your phrase and any brief, looks at documented references, and shows structurally different compositions rather than font swaps. It auditions the actual words in real font files, critiques at print scale, and will not reproduce a recognizable existing design or authorize publication.
design-sticker.overview: It works from your phrase and any brief, looks at documented references, and shows structurally different compositions rather than font swaps. It auditions the actual words in real font files, critiques at print scale, and will not reproduce a recognizable existing design or authorize publication.
design-sticker.value: Explore materially different typographic compositions for a sticker, then judge them at the size people will hold or read. It helps move beyond changing a font while leaving the same weak layout intact.

preparation.where: Provide the phrase or concept, intended print size and relevant collection or brand references. Actual font files are used for type auditions; production constraints come from your intended materials and process.
preparation.missing: You can begin with a phrase and brief. Missing source assets or print dimensions limit production-ready conclusions. A digital proof does not demonstrate physical print quality, and recognizable existing designs are not reproduced.

lay-out-sticker-sheets.what: Lay out the user’s sticker designs for Cricut printing.
lay-out-sticker-sheets.when: PNG designs need exact-count Print Then Cut sheets.
lay-out-sticker-sheets.inputs: The designs, requested sizes and counts, and the user’s project generator.
lay-out-sticker-sheets.outputs: Generated sheets and layout checks before a physical print test.
lay-out-sticker-sheets.example: Lay out these PNGs in the requested sizes and counts using my current sheet generator.
lay-out-sticker-sheets.reuseNote: Use the caller’s explicitly supplied or authorized sources, configuration, profile and destination. No personal identity or standing permissions transfer with the workflow.
lay-out-sticker-sheets.expect: It finds the project's sheet generator, reads its help, and confirms paper size separately from the cut area before laying out your PNGs. It runs with branding off unless you ask for a maker mark, then checks the manifest, contact sheet, DPI and every requested count, reporting any skipped duplicates.
lay-out-sticker-sheets.requires: The project's sheet generator script and the supplied PNG designs; if the generator is unavailable it asks for it instead of guessing.
lay-out-sticker-sheets.overview: It finds the project's sheet generator, reads its help, and confirms paper size separately from the cut area before laying out your PNGs. It runs with branding off unless you ask for a maker mark, then checks the manifest, contact sheet, DPI and every requested count, reporting any skipped duplicates.
lay-out-sticker-sheets.value: Place the requested quantities and sizes of PNG designs on Print Then Cut sheets and check the resulting inventory. It helps avoid a printable-looking sheet with the wrong counts, cut area or resolution.

preparation.where: Supply the PNGs, sizes, counts and your project's current sheet-generator script. The generator is an existing production tool in your project; it is not automatically included by this workflow. Paper size and usable cut area must be specified separately.
preparation.missing: If the generator is unavailable, supply it before generation. The workflow does not guess a replacement layout system. Generated sheets still need a physical alignment/print test before production is treated as verified.

preparationSkills.reason: Optional design work before layout when the source PNGs still need developing.

design-software-system.what: Explore a system or service design.
design-software-system.when: A working architecture or technical trade-off discussion is needed.
design-software-system.inputs: The problem, requirements, constraints, scale, and existing system context.
design-software-system.outputs: A working design covering components, data, interfaces, and trade-offs.
design-software-system.example: Explore a working design for this service, including its data flow and trade-offs.
design-software-system.expect: It states its assumptions, then walks requirements, components, data model, APIs, scaling and trade-offs, leading with a recommended design. It marks assumed scale or latency figures as assumed instead of inventing them, and points you to the formal architecture mode if you need a sourced reference.
design-software-system.overview: It states its assumptions, then walks requirements, components, data model, APIs, scaling and trade-offs, leading with a recommended design. It marks assumed scale or latency figures as assumed instead of inventing them, and points you to the formal architecture mode if you need a sourced reference.
design-software-system.value: Work through how a service or system could meet its requirements, including components, data, APIs, scale and trade-offs. It gives a recommended working design for discussion before a formal architecture reference is needed.

preparation.where: Describe the problem, users, requirements and constraints. For an existing system, provide the relevant code or diagrams. Scale and latency targets are supplied requirements or explicitly stated assumptions, not hidden defaults.
preparation.missing: No existing architecture document is required to explore a new design. Unknown requirements remain assumptions or decisions. Use the formal architecture-reference mode when you need a sourced record of settled design rather than an exploratory recommendation.

preparationSkills.reason: Produces a formal sourced reference once the design has sufficient decisions and evidence.

plan-team-onboarding.what: Plan a role’s first 30, 60, and 90 days.
plan-team-onboarding.when: A new starter or team transition needs a structured ramp.
plan-team-onboarding.inputs: The role, success criteria, mentors, existing materials, access, and time budget.
plan-team-onboarding.outputs: A role-specific onboarding plan with learning, contribution, and feedback milestones.
plan-team-onboarding.example: Create a 30/60/90-day plan for this role using the team’s mentoring and access constraints.
plan-team-onboarding.expect: It asks for the role, existing docs, who will mentor, the access needed and how much team time is available, then produces a pre-day-1 checklist, day-1 schedule, reading list, 30/60/90 milestones, buddy guide and retrospective template. It delivers in chat unless you ask for a file.
plan-team-onboarding.overview: It asks for the role, existing docs, who will mentor, the access needed and how much team time is available, then produces a pre-day-1 checklist, day-1 schedule, reading list, 30/60/90 milestones, buddy guide and retrospective template. It delivers in chat unless you ask for a file.
plan-team-onboarding.value: Make the first weeks in a role concrete: access, reading, mentoring, early contributions and feedback. It balances the new starter's learning with the time the existing team can actually provide.

preparation.where: Describe the role, expected outcomes, available mentors, existing team documents and access requirements. The 30/60/90 plan, buddy guide and checklists are outputs; you do not need to author those first.
preparation.missing: Missing role expectations, access owners or mentoring capacity become questions to resolve. It can deliver the plan in chat without a file tool; it cannot provision accounts or confirm access that has not been granted.

ingest-transcript.what: Preserve and index a meeting transcript.
ingest-transcript.when: A transcript or recording export needs a durable project record.
ingest-transcript.inputs: The original transcript and confirmed client, opportunity, or engagement identity.
ingest-transcript.outputs: A preserved source, normalized transcript, and indexed meeting record.
ingest-transcript.example: Preserve and index this transcript under its confirmed opportunity and meeting identity.
ingest-transcript.expect: It confirms the client and an opportunity or engagement ID before filing and stops if the meeting could belong to more than one. It keeps the raw transcript untouched, writes a normalized copy and index entry, and proposes claims with locators that go through the evidence step rather than being promoted directly.
ingest-transcript.requires: A transcript file (Markdown, text or VTT), a confirmed client and opp- or eng- context ID, and Python 3 for the normalizer on a local machine.
ingest-transcript.overview: It confirms the client and an opportunity or engagement ID before filing and stops if the meeting could belong to more than one. It keeps the raw transcript untouched, writes a normalized copy and index entry, and proposes claims with locators that go through the evidence step rather than being promoted directly.
ingest-transcript.value: Preserve a meeting's original words and make the transcript discoverable under the right project. It creates a normalized reading copy and index without replacing the raw evidence or turning every remark into a confirmed requirement.

preparation.where: Supply a Markdown, text or VTT transcript and confirm the client plus opportunity or engagement ID. That ID is your project's filing identity. It comes from the project/CRM record or owner, not from a guessed client-name match.
preparation.missing: Ambiguous identity stops filing. With no transcript, recording export or supported text, the normalizer cannot run. Claims extracted from a transcript still need the evidence step before being treated as accepted project facts.

validate-delivery.what: Trace tests to requirements, track UAT and assemble the go or no-go evidence.
validate-delivery.when: Testing starts, or someone asks for test scripts, coverage or whether the release is ready.
validate-delivery.inputs: The requirements workbook, the Test Plan, the SOW acceptance section, build status and reported test results.
validate-delivery.outputs: Traced test scripts, a defect log, a UAT tracker with coverage, and a go or no-go pack with an empty decision block.
validate-delivery.example: Build the test scripts and traceability check from this requirements workbook.
validate-delivery.expect: It finds the requirements workbook, Test Plan and SOW acceptance language first and stops with a gap memo if one is missing. It builds traced test scripts, a UAT tracker, defect log and a go/no-go pack whose counts a script recomputes; humans execute tests, triage and decide, and the decision block stays empty.
validate-delivery.requires: The requirements workbook with requirement IDs, the Test Plan and the SOW acceptance section, plus Python 3 for the traceability gate.
validate-delivery.overview: It finds the requirements workbook, Test Plan and SOW acceptance language first and stops with a gap memo if one is missing. It builds traced test scripts, a UAT tracker, defect log and a go/no-go pack whose counts a script recomputes; humans execute tests, triage and decide, and the decision block stays empty.
validate-delivery.value: Connect tests and UAT results to requirements and contractual acceptance. It shows coverage, defects and remaining release decisions so a finished build is not confused with an accepted delivery.

preparation.where: Supply requirements with IDs, the Test Plan, SOW acceptance language, build status and reported test results. The workbook normally comes from Capture requirements; the Test Plan specifies coverage and approach. These documents come from the engagement, not from the validator's assumptions.
preparation.missing: If a required document is missing, it returns a gap memo. It prepares scripts, trackers and a go/no-go pack, but humans execute tests and make the release decision; the decision block is left for them.

preparationSkills.reason: Provides the requirements workbook and stable IDs used for test traceability.

plan-usability-study.what: Plan usability research or synthesize observations.
plan-usability-study.when: A team needs participant tasks, sessions, or findings.
plan-usability-study.inputs: The research questions, interface, participant context, and supplied observations.
plan-usability-study.outputs: A session plan, neutral task scripts, or supported usability findings.
plan-usability-study.example: Write neutral participant tasks for these research questions and this interface.
plan-usability-study.expect: It starts from the decision the research should inform, then writes a session plan with neutral task wording or synthesizes the observations you supply. It keeps what participants said, what was observed and interpretation separate, and returns a plan or labeled provisional findings rather than inventing participants, quotes or success rates.
plan-usability-study.overview: It starts from the decision the research should inform, then writes a session plan with neutral task wording or synthesizes the observations you supply. It keeps what participants said, what was observed and interpretation separate, and returns a plan or labeled provisional findings rather than inventing participants, quotes or success rates.
plan-usability-study.value: Learn whether people can complete the tasks the product is meant to support. It turns a research question into neutral participant tasks or organizes supplied observations into findings that can guide a decision.

preparation.where: Provide the decision to inform, target interface, participant context and research questions. For synthesis, supply actual session notes or observations. A research plan is an output; recorded sessions are only required when asking for findings from completed research.
preparation.missing: With no observations it can prepare a study, not report participant outcomes. Thin evidence produces provisional findings. Participants, quotations and success rates cannot be invented to complete a report.

review-writing.what: Review prose for clarity, meaning, and the intended voice.
review-writing.when: Writing needs drafting, revision, review, or a retained correction.
review-writing.inputs: The brief or draft, controlling sources, and an authorized profile when available.
review-writing.outputs: Complete reviewed prose and, when enabled, private correction-learning records.
review-writing.example: Review this draft for clarity, repetition, and unsupported claims. Preserve its meaning and intended voice; return the complete revision.
review-writing.expect: It reviews your text for meaning, structure and sentence patterns, returns complete edits, and keeps quotations, figures and executable syntax exact. Learned preferences are loaded and saved only from a private profile store you have authorized, and it reports a saved correction only when it has a storage receipt.
review-writing.overview: It reads the whole draft for meaning and structure, repairs vague or repetitive passages and sentence patterns, and returns complete revised text while preserving facts, uncertainty, quotations and executable syntax. Available diagnostic tools support the reading review with pattern and figure checks. Optional preference learning uses only an authorized private profile store. For HTML pages, workbooks, documents and decks, it reviews the extracted text line by line, fixes each finding at its source and writes a coverage receipt.
review-writing.value: Improve a draft's meaning, structure and wording while preserving facts, uncertainty and the intended author. It returns the full revised text rather than leaving the writer to assemble a list of isolated edits.

preparation.where: Provide the draft or writing brief and sources needed to preserve its claims. An authorized private profile is optional for learned preferences; ordinary review uses the core rules without a profile store. Saved files and Python are needed for executable diagnostics, not for a manual text review.
preparation.missing: Without source evidence, unsupported claims must be identified rather than reinforced. Without an authorized profile, it does not load or save learned preferences. Unavailable scanner checks remain unperformed even when the text is reviewed manually.

manage-writing-profile.what: Build or revise a person’s private writing profile.
manage-writing-profile.when: Someone authorizes a profile from their writing samples.
manage-writing-profile.inputs: Authorized samples, the intended author, profile scope, and confirmation.
manage-writing-profile.outputs: A reviewed private profile with supported style rules and update controls.
manage-writing-profile.example: Build a draft style profile from these authorized samples and identify the rules I need to confirm.
manage-writing-profile.expect: It asks whose voice, from which sources and for what purpose, and stops without that authorization even if a mail or chat connector is available. It uses only material the person wrote, shows the proposed profile for confirmation before saving it, and declines to build one when the evidence is too thin.
manage-writing-profile.requires: Explicit authorization from the person being profiled and material they supply or authorize; Python 3 runs the profile builder.
manage-writing-profile.overview: It asks whose voice, from which sources and for what purpose, and stops without that authorization even if a mail or chat connector is available. It uses only material the person wrote, shows the proposed profile for confirmation before saving it, and declines to build one when the evidence is too thin.
manage-writing-profile.value: Build a reusable account of how a particular person writes, grounded in samples they authorize. It separates confirmed preferences from guesses so later drafting does not imitate a generic persona.

preparation.where: Identify the author, intended uses and writing samples the person actually wrote and permits you to use. A profile store is a private destination for the confirmed profile; a mail or chat connection does not itself grant permission to use its contents as samples.
preparation.missing: Without authorization or enough suitable evidence, profile creation stops. Proposed rules need confirmation before saving. You can still use ordinary writing review without creating a personal profile.

import-tracker-export.what: Turn a tracker export into canonical tickets, an intake record and a delta.
import-tracker-export.when: A new Jira or other tracker export arrives and later work needs to know what changed.
import-tracker-export.inputs: The export file or connector tickets, the engagement site.json, and who supplied the export and what it covers.
import-tracker-export.outputs: tickets.json, delta.json and an intake-log.json record with hash, origin, scope, redactions and conflicts.
import-tracker-export.example: Here is this week's Jira export; record it and tell me what changed since last Tuesday.
import-tracker-export.expect: It asks for the export plus who supplied it and what it covers, then converts it to canonical tickets and a delta against the previous export. It reports counts and every conflict such as an unknown status, drops comments and assignees, and does not change tickets in the tracker.
import-tracker-export.requires: Python 3, a tracker export (Jira CSV, table CSV or JSON), and the engagement's site.json config.
import-tracker-export.overview: It asks for the export plus who supplied it and what it covers, then converts it to canonical tickets and a delta against the previous export. It reports counts and every conflict such as an unknown status, drops comments and assignees, and does not change tickets in the tracker.
import-tracker-export.value: Make successive tracker exports comparable. It normalizes tickets and records what was supplied, which statuses could not be mapped and what changed, so later release views use a traceable snapshot.

preparation.where: Provide a Jira CSV, table CSV or JSON export with its supplier and coverage. The engagement's config/site.json defines how that project maps fields and statuses; it belongs to the review-site project folder and is not a universal tracker setting.
preparation.missing: Without the project mapping, ambiguous fields or statuses remain conflicts to resolve. A live connector is optional when an export is provided. Importing the file does not edit tickets in Jira or another tracker.

preparationSkills.reason: Uses the normalized tickets and intake records in the release review pages.

build-moscow-story-map.what: Keep a MoSCoW story map whose statuses, estimates and readiness come from the tracker.
build-moscow-story-map.when: A release backlog needs classing, a readiness view or a critical path, or new tickets need mapping after an export.
build-moscow-story-map.inputs: content/stories.json, canonical tickets and, after an export, delta.json.
build-moscow-story-map.outputs: A summary with readiness, Must share, unclassed tickets and the critical path, plus a review queue and class-review exports.
build-moscow-story-map.example: Which Must stories are not ready to build, and what blocks them?
build-moscow-story-map.expect: It reads the release's tickets and the client's workflow steps, asks you to supply the client's own class definitions, and writes the judgment fields of the story map. A script then computes readiness, Must share, unclassed tickets and the critical path from the tracker export, and class changes go through review instead of silent edits.
build-moscow-story-map.requires: Needs an engagement project folder with tracker/tickets.json from a tracker export, config/site.json holding the client's class definitions, and Python 3.
build-moscow-story-map.overview: It reads the release's tickets and the client's workflow steps, asks you to supply the client's own class definitions, and writes the judgment fields of the story map. A script then computes readiness, Must share, unclassed tickets and the critical path from the tracker export, and class changes go through review instead of silent edits.
build-moscow-story-map.value: Show how release work maps to the client's workflow, which Must items are not ready and what blocks the critical path. It calculates readiness from the tracker snapshot while keeping classification judgments reviewable.

preparation.where: Use canonical tracker/tickets.json, content/stories.json and config/site.json in the review-site engagement folder. Import tracker export prepares the ticket snapshot. Site configuration holds the client's own MoSCoW class definitions; the stories file holds the workflow mapping.
preparation.missing: Missing class definitions must come from the client; they are not invented by renaming generic priorities. Missing tickets require an import first. Classification changes enter a review queue instead of silently altering tracker data.

preparationSkills.reason: Prepares canonical tickets and the delta from the tracker export.

manage-decision-register.what: Keep refinement questions with owners, statuses and answers, and export them for the tracker.
manage-decision-register.when: Refinement or discovery produced open questions that need owners, answers and a record.
manage-decision-register.inputs: content/questions.json and, for exports, the answers saved on the published page.
manage-decision-register.outputs: A checked register, decisions.csv for tracker import and a decision log in Markdown.
manage-decision-register.example: Add the questions from today's refinement notes and list the ones with no owner.
manage-decision-register.expect: It turns questions from your meeting notes or refinement sources into register entries grouped by epic, with a status and an owner only when the sources name one. It reports unknown groups and questions without an owner, and it asks before writing anything to a tracker.
manage-decision-register.requires: Needs the project's content folder with the questions file, the published Decisions page for saved answers, and python3.
manage-decision-register.overview: It turns questions from your meeting notes or refinement sources into register entries grouped by epic, with a status and an owner only when the sources name one. It reports unknown groups and questions without an owner, and it asks before writing anything to a tracker.
manage-decision-register.value: Keep refinement questions actionable by connecting each one to its epic, owner, status and answer. It produces a register and exports people can use to reconcile decisions back to the tracker.

preparation.where: Bring meeting/refinement notes or the existing content/questions.json in the review-site project. For exports of collected answers, use the saved answers from the published Decisions page. An empty or unassigned question is retained as unresolved.
preparation.missing: You can start by extracting questions from notes. Missing owners stay missing rather than inferred. Without access to saved page answers, it cannot claim to include them; tracker writes require a separate authorized operation.

preparationSkills.reason: Publishes the Decisions page where the team can review the register.

build-review-site.what: Build or refresh a multi-page release review site from tracker exports and content files.
build-review-site.when: A client team reviews a release backlog with MoSCoW classes, open decisions, workflows and build steps.
build-review-site.inputs: An engagement folder with site.json, content files and tracker exports, plus the brand profile when one is confirmed.
build-review-site.outputs: A gated, rendered site published as a private artifact, comment replies, and CSV exports for the tracker.
build-review-site.example: Refresh the review site with the new Jira export and republish it.
build-review-site.expect: It builds or refreshes a multi-page review site from a tracker export and content files in an engagement folder. Gates check references, data and writing and a failing writing gate blocks publishing; after they pass you are expected to read each page, and publishing needs a live-artifact check so another writer's changes are not overwritten.
build-review-site.requires: Needs an engagement folder with a tracker export and Python 3; browser checks need Playwright's Chromium, and publishing needs the artifact tools with the shared database capability.
build-review-site.overview: It builds or refreshes a multi-page review site from a tracker export and content files in an engagement folder. Gates check references, data and writing and a failing writing gate blocks publishing; after they pass you are expected to read each page, and publishing needs a live-artifact check so another writer's changes are not overwritten.
build-review-site.value: Give a client team one place to review release scope, readiness, open decisions and build steps. It combines tracker snapshots and curated content into linked pages with data and writing checks before publication.

preparation.where: Use an engagement folder containing config/site.json, content files and tracker exports. The related import, story-map and decision-register workflows prepare those records. Python builds locally; browser checks and hosted publishing need the supported runtime and artifact capabilities.
preparation.missing: A missing export or configuration must be prepared before a reliable build. A local site can be built without a publishing connection, but cannot be called published. Existing live changes must be checked before replacing the hosted artifact.

preparationSkills.reason: Prepares traceable ticket snapshots.
Maintains the workflow/classification and readiness view.
Maintains refinement questions and recorded answers.

review-site-runtime.what: Shared runtime for the build-review-site skills: data contract, calculations, page templates and gates.
review-site-runtime.when: One of the build-review-site skills runs; it is not selected on its own.
review-site-runtime.inputs: Engagement config, content files and canonical tickets passed by the calling skill.
review-site-runtime.outputs: Computed page data, the rendered site and gate results.
review-site-runtime.example: Loaded by build-review-site when it renders and checks the site.
review-site-runtime.expect: It is an internal runtime used by the build-review-site skills and has no entrypoint of its own, so you reach it through import-tracker-export, build-moscow-story-map, manage-decision-register or build-review-site. Page and rule changes are made in its source templates, never in a rendered output folder.
review-site-runtime.requires: Needs Python 3 for its library, and Node.js with Playwright for the browser checks.
review-site-runtime.overview: It is an internal runtime used by the build-review-site skills and has no entrypoint of its own, so you reach it through import-tracker-export, build-moscow-story-map, manage-decision-register or build-review-site. Page and rule changes are made in its source templates, never in a rendered output folder.
review-site-runtime.value: Supply the common data calculations, page templates and gates used by the release review-site workflows. Sharing this runtime keeps ticket counts and readiness rules consistent across the import, story map, decision page and full site.

preparation.where: The calling workflow supplies engagement configuration, content and canonical tickets. Python executes the library; Node and Playwright support its browser checks. Use Import tracker export, Build MoSCoW story map, Manage decision register or Build review site rather than selecting the runtime alone.
preparation.missing: Without the project's data/configuration, the runtime cannot create meaningful pages. Template changes belong in the maintained source; editing generated pages would be lost on the next build.

preparationSkills.reason: Select this producing workflow to build the full review site.

build-editorial-chart.what: Build an editorial chart or small dashboard from supplied numbers, with the finding in the headline, one highlighted series and direct labels.
build-editorial-chart.when: Numbers with a known source need a chart that reads clearly on a phone and a desktop, including progress against plan, estimate ranges and targets.
build-editorial-chart.inputs: The numbers with their source, unit and timeframe, the finding or question, and optionally a brand profile.
build-editorial-chart.outputs: A self-contained HTML chart page in light and dark themes, checked by check_html.py.
build-editorial-chart.example: Chart these phase hours, planned against used, and highlight the workstream that hasn't started.
build-editorial-chart.expect: It picks the chart type, writes a JSON spec or D3 panel, renders the page in the selected brand profile (the neutral profile by default), runs the HTML check, and inspects the page at desktop width and 375px. It uses only the supplied numbers, draws targets and projections dashed, and keeps any hosted page private.
build-editorial-chart.requires: Python 3 for the scripts, Node for the inline script syntax check, and a browser for the visual check.
build-editorial-chart.overview: It chooses an appropriate chart for your question, prepares a data specification or interactive panel and renders an HTML page with direct labels, a finding-led headline and one highlighted series. Targets and projections are styled differently from actuals. It checks the HTML and inspects desktop and phone layouts; chart data must come from your supplied numbers.
build-editorial-chart.value: Show the finding in supplied numbers with direct labels and enough context to read the chart without hovering. It is useful for progress against plan, estimate ranges or actuals against targets where a default chart would obscure the comparison.

preparation.where: Provide numbers, units, timeframe and the source, plus the question or finding to explain. A chart JSON specification is the structured input it prepares. Python builds the page; Node checks inline scripts and a browser is needed for visual inspection.
preparation.missing: No separate analytics plan is required when the numbers and question already exist. Missing measurements cannot be generated by drawing a chart. The resulting HTML loads pinned chart libraries online, and web fonts only for a brand font or the newsroom look, so viewing is not fully offline; hosting does not imply permission to share.

preparationSkills.reason: Use this if you need to define measurements; it is unnecessary when chart-ready data already exists.

writing.what: Write or review every word a person will read against the owner's writing rules folder, with a check that proves which lines it covered.
writing.when: Any reply, document, page, deck, message, interface label, commit message or pull request description is about to go to a reader, or another tool needs a pass or fail on a saved file. Use review-writing until this skill's three proof runs are done.
writing.inputs: The draft or the saved file, the writing rules folder, and the channel and audience for the piece.
writing.outputs: The reviewed text, and for a saved file a JSON result with status, line coverage, findings and a receipt.
writing.example: Check this proposal page before it goes to the client, then run the full review with the line pass and the document pass.
writing.expect: It reads the rules from the owner's folder each time, picks review, owner voice or brand voice, and sets the register from the channel and audience. For a file, check.py extracts the reader text, scans every in-scope line in parts of at most 300 lines and exits 0, 1 or 2. A full review adds a verdict for every line, a claims answer checked against a source list, a document map and a spot audit, and the script rejects a missing verdict, a misquoted line or an untraced number. Code and quotations are exempt.
writing.requires: Python 3 for check.py, and a writing rules folder with patterns.json named by --rules-dir, WRITING_HOME or the path in ~/.agents/writing/home.
writing.overview: It loads the owner's writing rules from their folder for each task and carries no copy of them. For a draft it picks the mode and register, then reviews each line. For a saved file, check.py extracts the text a reader sees, exempts code and quotations, scans every in-scope line and writes a receipt that counts the lines scanned against the lines extracted. A full review adds a verdict for every line and a document map that the script validates.
writing.value: Give other tools one command that returns pass, fail or incomplete for a file, and stop a review from being reported as done when lines were skipped.

preparation.where: Provide the draft or the file path, and a writing rules folder that holds patterns.json. Name the folder with --rules-dir, the WRITING_HOME variable or the path in ~/.agents/writing/home. A full review also needs rules.md in that folder, a JSON list of the source documents and the project's confidentiality list from the Hub.
preparation.missing: With no pattern ledger the check exits 2. With no rules.md the scan still runs and a full review is reported incomplete. A format the script does not read exits 2.

publish-content.what: Take a piece of content from topic to publishable draft through nine gated steps, or rebuild an AI-written draft into one that can be published.
publish-content.when: Someone wants blog posts, newsletters, guides, news, reviews, case studies or proposals that rest on the owner's own evidence, or has an AI draft to rescue or retire.
publish-content.inputs: A goal for the run or the draft to rescue, a filled owner profile, the owner's writing rules folder, and the owner's data, answers and permissions.
publish-content.outputs: The final draft with its exhibits, a claim table, a meaning diff, panel scores, an approval packet, a run ledger entry and the defect log.
publish-content.example: Write a portfolio case study about the pricing rebuild from my decision notes and the before and after numbers, and stop for my sign-off before anything is published.
publish-content.expect: Separate agents scout topics, research, collect the owner's evidence, brief, draft, build exhibits, edit, fact-check and score the draft, and each step has a gate. It stops at every human gate with an approval packet. evidence_scan.py and the owner's writing check run at steps 6 and 9, and a claim with no source is cut, not softened. Nothing is published without the owner's sign-off.
publish-content.requires: Python 3 for evidence_scan.py, web research for the scout and researcher, and the owner's writing rules folder for the editor.
publish-content.overview: It runs a topic through nine steps, each owned by one agent with its own procedure. Every section of the brief needs a claim and an evidence ID, exhibits are built as code from cited data, and the editor removes AI writing patterns before a fact checker and a reader panel see the draft. Case studies also produce an evidence file that a named person signs.
publish-content.value: Publish pieces that carry the owner's own evidence and decisions, and refuse pieces that do not. The pipeline sets no volume target, and a topic with nothing only the owner holds is dropped at step 2.

preparation.where: Fill the owner profile template and pass its path. Name the writing rules folder in the profile, and supply the owner's data files, screenshots, permissions and answers when the asset collector asks.
preparation.missing: Without an owner profile the run stops and asks for one. Without the writing rules folder the editor uses the general layers and says the owner's rules did not run. Without web research the scout and researcher use only owner-supplied material.

preparationSkills.reason: Use this to build the owner's voice profile when pieces go out under the owner's name and no profile exists yet.
